claim: Patients with recessive myotonia congenita (Becker disease) experience debilitating bouts of transient weakness.
source: In addition to the hallmark muscle stiffness, patients with recessive myotonia congenita (Becker disease) experience debilitating bouts of transient weakness that remain poorly understood despite years of study.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a known clinical feature of the disease.

claim: Transient weakness in Becker disease has remained poorly understood despite years of study.
source: In addition to the hallmark muscle stiffness, patients with recessive myotonia congenita (Becker disease) experience debilitating bouts of transient weakness that remain poorly understood despite years of study.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as background context.

claim: Intracellular recordings from genetic and pharmacologic mouse models of Becker disease reveal transient depolarizations (plateau potentials) of the membrane potential to −25 to −35 mV.
source: Our recordings reveal transient depolarizations (plateau potentials) of the membrane potential to −25 to −35 mV in the genetic and pharmacologic models of Becker disease.
evidence: This is a primary finding reported in the abstract based on experimental recordings.

claim: Both Na+ and Ca2+ currents contribute to plateau potentials.
source: Both Na+ and Ca2+ currents contribute to plateau potentials.
evidence: This is stated as a finding in the abstract.

claim: Na+ persistent inward current (NaPIC) through NaV1.4 channels is the key trigger of plateau potentials.
source: Na+ persistent inward current (NaPIC) through NaV1.4 channels is the key trigger of plateau potentials and current through CaV1.1 Ca2+ channels contributes to the duration of the plateau.
evidence: This is stated as a finding in the abstract based on experimental data.

claim: Current through CaV1.1 Ca2+ channels contributes to the duration of plateau potentials.
source: Na+ persistent inward current (NaPIC) through NaV1.4 channels is the key trigger of plateau potentials and current through CaV1.1 Ca2+ channels contributes to the duration of the plateau.
evidence: This is stated as a finding in the abstract based on experimental data.

claim: Inhibiting NaPIC with ranolazine prevents the development of plateau potentials.
source: Inhibiting NaPIC with ranolazine prevents the development of plateau potentials and eliminates transient weakness in vivo.
evidence: This is stated as a finding in the abstract based on experimental data.

claim: Inhibiting NaPIC with ranolazine eliminates transient weakness in vivo.
source: Inhibiting NaPIC with ranolazine prevents the development of plateau potentials and eliminates transient weakness in vivo.
evidence: This is stated as a finding in the abstract based on experimental data.

claim: Targeting NaPIC may be an effective treatment to prevent transient weakness in myotonia congenita.
source: These data suggest that targeting NaPIC may be an effective treatment to prevent transient weakness in myotonia congenita.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental findings with ranolazine.

claim: Myotonia congenita is caused by loss-of-function mutations affecting the muscle chloride channel (ClC-1).
source: It is caused by loss-of-function mutations affecting the muscle chloride channel (ClC-1) (Lipicky et al., 1971; Steinmeyer et al., 1991; Koch et al., 1992).
evidence: This is stated with supporting citations to prior literature.

claim: Patients with Becker disease experience muscle stiffness due to hyperexcitability.
source: Patients with recessive myotonia congenita (Becker disease) experience muscle stiffness due to hyperexcitability (Lehmann-Horn et al., 2008; Trivedi et al., 2014; Cannon, 2015) as well as transient weakness due to unknown factors (Ricker et al., 1978; Rüdel et al., 1988; Zwarts and van Weerden, 1989; Deymeer et al., 1998; the CINCH Consortium et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated with supporting citations to prior literature.

claim: Some patients with Becker disease report transient weakness in arm muscles as a greater impediment than muscle stiffness.
source: Some patients with Becker disease report transient weakness in arm muscles as a greater impediment than muscle stiffness (Rüdel et al., 1988).
evidence: This is stated with a supporting citation to prior literature.

claim: Transient weakness in Becker disease can last up to 90 s.
source: This weakness can last up to 90 s and is brought on by exertion following rest (Ricker et al., 1978; Rüdel et al., 1988; Zwarts and van Weerden, 1989; Deymeer et al., 1998).
evidence: This is stated with supporting citations to prior literature.

claim: Transient weakness in Becker disease is brought on by exertion following rest.
source: This weakness can last up to 90 s and is brought on by exertion following rest (Ricker et al., 1978; Rüdel et al., 1988; Zwarts and van Weerden, 1989; Deymeer et al., 1998).
evidence: This is stated with supporting citations to prior literature.

claim: The mechanism underlying transient weakness in Becker disease has remained unknown since its initial description close to 50 years ago.
source: The mechanism underlying transient weakness in Becker disease has remained unknown since its initial description close to 50 years ago (Ricker and Meinck, 1972).
evidence: This is stated with a supporting citation to prior literature.

claim: Weakness in Becker disease is accompanied by a drop in compound muscle action potential (CMAP) amplitude during repetitive stimulation.
source: There appears to be loss of muscle excitability, as weakness is accompanied by a drop in compound muscle action potential (CMAP) amplitude during repetitive stimulation (Ricker and Meinck, 1972; Brown, 1974; Aminoff et al., 1977; Deymeer et al., 1998; Drost et al., 2001; Modoni et al., 2011).
evidence: This is stated with supporting citations to prior literature.

claim: The drop in CMAP in Becker disease is associated with reduction in muscle fiber conduction velocity.
source: This drop in CMAP is associated with reduction in muscle fiber conduction velocity, which has been proposed to progress to depolarization block (Zwarts and van Weerden, 1989).
evidence: This is stated with a supporting citation to prior literature.

claim: Reduction in muscle fiber conduction velocity has been proposed to progress to depolarization block in Becker disease.
source: This drop in CMAP is associated with reduction in muscle fiber conduction velocity, which has been proposed to progress to depolarization block (Zwarts and van Weerden, 1989).
evidence: This is stated with a supporting citation to prior literature.

claim: The ClCadr mouse model of Becker disease has transient weakness in vivo.
source: We established that a ClC-1 homozygous null (ClCadr) mouse model of Becker disease has transient weakness in vivo, mimicking the condition in human patients.
evidence: This is stated as a finding established by the authors.

claim: The ClCadr mouse model mimics the transient weakness condition in human patients with Becker disease.
source: We established that a ClC-1 homozygous null (ClCadr) mouse model of Becker disease has transient weakness in vivo, mimicking the condition in human patients.
evidence: This is stated as a finding established by the authors.

claim: Plateau potentials are the mechanism underlying transient weakness in Becker disease.
source: We conclude that NaPIC plays a central role in the development of plateau potentials, which are the mechanism underlying transient weakness in Becker disease.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion drawn from the experimental findings.

claim: In unaffected littermates, stimulation with 45 pulses at 100 Hz causes no myotonia and immediate relaxation.
source: In unaffected littermates, there was no myotonia following 45 pulses at 100 Hz, such that relaxation was immediate (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 1A.

claim: In ClCadr mice, stimulation with 45 pulses causes full fusion of force but relaxation is slowed due to myotonia.
source: In ClCadr mice, stimulation with 45 pulses caused full fusion of force, but relaxation was slowed, due to the presence of myotonia (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 1C.

claim: In unaffected littermates, stimulation with 15 pulses at 100 Hz every 4 s for 1 min causes stable force production with a mild, gradual reduction likely due to fatigue.
source: In unaffected littermates, this caused stable force production with a mild, gradual reduction that was likely due to fatigue (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 1B.

claim: In myotonic mice, stimulation with 15 pulses at 100 Hz every 4 s reveals transient weakness, as force falls over the first 10–15 s and then recovers.
source: In myotonic mice, the same stimulation protocol revealed transient weakness, as force fell over the first 10–15 s and then recovered (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Transient weakness in ClCadr mice peaks in severity 15–20 s after the initial stimulation and resolves within 1 min.
source: The plot of the mean normalized force revealed transient weakness, which peaked in severity 15–20 s after the initial stimulation and resolved within 1 min (Figure 1E).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 1E.

claim: In muscle from unaffected littermates, firing of action potentials ceases as soon as the stimulus is terminated.
source: In both unaffected littermates and ClCadr mice, stimulation with a 200 ms injection of depolarizing current triggered repetitive firing of action potentials during the stimulus. In muscle from unaffected littermates, the firing ceased as soon as the stimulus was terminated (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 2A.

claim: In muscle from ClCadr mice, there is myotonia (continued firing of action potentials following termination of the stimulus) in 100% of fibers.
source: In muscle from ClCadr mice, there was myotonia (continued firing of action potentials following termination of the stimulus) in 100% of fibers (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 2B.

claim: In ClCadr muscle, myotonia often persists for many seconds.
source: The myotonia often persisted for many seconds.
evidence: This is stated in the text describing the experimental observations.

claim: In some instances in ClCadr muscle, myotonia terminates with the development of depolarizations lasting 5 to >100 s to a membrane potential near −35 mV.
source: While most runs of myotonia ended with repolarization to the resting membrane potential (Figure 2B), in some instances, myotonia terminated with the development of depolarizations lasting 5 to >100 s to a membrane potential near −35 mV (Figure 2C,D).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figures 2C and 2D.

claim: During prolonged depolarizations in ClCadr muscle, there is a gradual repolarization of the membrane to near −45 mV, followed by sudden repolarization back to the resting potential.
source: During these prolonged depolarizations, there was a gradual repolarization of the membrane to near −45 mV, followed by sudden repolarization back to the resting potential.
evidence: This is stated in the text describing the experimental observations.

claim: In some cases, the sudden repolarization is preceded by the development of oscillations in the membrane potential.
source: In some cases, the sudden repolarization was preceded by the development of oscillations in the membrane potential (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 2D.

claim: Prolonged depolarizations (plateau potentials) occurred in 30% of ClCadr muscle fibers.
source: The prolonged depolarizations occurred in 30% of ClCadr muscle fibers (n = 36/119 fibers from 10 mice).
evidence: This is stated in the text with specific numbers from the experiments.

claim: Of the 36 ClCadr fibers with plateau potentials, 26 repolarized to within 4 mV of their initial resting potential.
source: Of the 36 fibers with plateau potentials, 26 repolarized to within 4 mV of their initial resting potential.
evidence: This is stated in the text with specific numbers from the experiments.

claim: During and immediately following plateau potentials, action potential generation in response to current injection fails.
source: During and immediately following plateau potentials, action potential generation in response to current injection failed (Figure 2E).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 2E.

claim: At later times following repolarization from plateau potentials, action potential generation is again possible.
source: At later times following repolarization, action potential generation was again possible.
evidence: This is stated in the text describing the experimental observations.

claim: The inexcitability at earlier times following repolarization from plateau potentials is likely due to slow inactivation of Na channels following the many-second depolarization.
source: The inexcitability at earlier times following repolarization is likely due to slow inactivation of Na channels following the many-second depolarization (Ruff, 1996; Ruff, 1999; Rich and Pinter, 2003).
evidence: This is stated as an interpretation with supporting citations.

claim: Acute blocking of ClC-1 with 100 µM 9-AC triggers myotonia and plateau potentials in 92% of fibers from unaffected littermates.
source: Acute blocking of ClC-1 triggered myotonia and plateau potentials in 92% of fibers (Figure 3A, 49/53 fibers from eight mice).
evidence: This is stated in the text with specific numbers and shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Following acute block of ClC-1 channels with 9-AC, all plateau potentials terminated with sudden repolarization to within 4 mV of the previous resting potential.
source: Following acute block of ClC-1 channels with 9-AC, all plateau potentials terminated with sudden repolarization to within 4 mV of the previous resting potential (49/49 fibers).
evidence: This is stated in the text with specific numbers from the experiments.

claim: The ion channels responsible for development of plateau potentials are present in wild-type skeletal muscle.
source: These data strongly suggest that the ion channels responsible for development of plateau potentials are present in wild-type skeletal muscle.
evidence: This is stated as an inference from the 9-AC experiments.

claim: The duration of plateau potentials in ClCadr and 9-AC models is highly variable.
source: In contrast to the relative consistency in voltage at onset and termination of plateau potentials, the duration in both the ClCadr and 9-AC treated models of myotonia was highly variable (Figure 3B, Table 1, variance = 3131 s for ClCadr and 623 s for 9-AC treated muscles).
evidence: This is stated in the text with specific variance values and shown in Figure 3B and Table 1.

claim: The rate of repolarization during plateau potentials varies by more than 100-fold.
source: The reason for the high variance of duration was that the rate of repolarization during the plateau potential varied by more than 100-fold (Figure 3B, Table 1).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 3B and Table 1.

claim: Within individual 9-AC treated fibers, the slope of repolarization of plateau potentials is less variable such that duration is relatively constant with a mean variance of 0.5 s ± 0.7 s.
source: Within individual fibers, the slope of repolarization of plateau potentials was less variable such that duration was relatively constant with a mean variance of 0.5 s ± 0.7 s (n = 17 9-AC treated fibers in which four or more plateau potentials were recorded).
evidence: This is stated in the text with specific numbers from the experiments.

claim: In 9-AC treated fibers, the mean membrane potential during the final 500 ms of runs of myotonia is more depolarized in runs that produce plateau potentials compared to runs that do not.
source: In 22/22 fibers, the mean membrane potential was more depolarized in runs of myotonia that produced plateau potentials (mean = −40.1 ± 3.1 mV vs −49.0 ± 4.5 mV, p=5 × 10−11, paired t-test, Figure 3D).
evidence: This is stated in the text with specific values and statistical analysis, and shown in Figure 3D.

claim: In 9-AC treated fibers, the mean firing rate during the final 500 ms of runs of myotonia is higher for runs ending in plateau potentials compared to runs ending with repolarization.
source: In 21/22 fibers, the mean firing rate was higher for runs of myotonia ending in plateau potentials (mean = 31.2 ± 5.7 Hz vs 23.4 ± 2.9, p=7 × 10−6, paired t-test, Figure 3E).
evidence: This is stated in the text with specific values and statistical analysis, and shown in Figure 3E.

claim: Membrane conductance is increased by 50% during the early phase of plateau potentials compared to baseline.
source: Since the response appeared passive during the early phase of plateau potentials we estimated relative input resistance, which was reduced by 50% following initial depolarization versus baseline (0.43 ± 0.05 vs 0.90 ± 0.12 MΩ, p<0.01, paired t-test, n = 14 fibers).
evidence: This is stated in the text with specific values and statistical analysis.

claim: There is a net increase in membrane conductance during the early phase of plateau potentials.
source: While caution must be used in interpreting these data, they favor the possibility that there is a net increase in membrane conductance during the early phase of plateau potentials.
evidence: This is stated as an interpretation of the input resistance measurements.

claim: Application of 100 µM 9-AC led to the development of plateau potentials in 41/49 fibers from four wild-type mice.
source: Application of 100 µM 9-AC led to the development of plateau potentials in 41/49 fibers from four wild-type mice and in 47/49 fibers from three ncDHPR mice (Figure 6D and E).
evidence: This is stated in the text with specific numbers and shown in Figures 6D and 6E.

claim: Application of 100 µM 9-AC led to the development of plateau potentials in 47/49 fibers from three ncDHPR mice.
source: Application of 100 µM 9-AC led to the development of plateau potentials in 41/49 fibers from four wild-type mice and in 47/49 fibers from three ncDHPR mice (Figure 6D and E).
evidence: This is stated in the text with specific numbers and shown in Figures 6D and 6E.

claim: Ca2+ influx through Cav1.1 does not play a role in the initiation of plateau potentials.
source: These data suggest that Ca2+ influx through Cav1.1 does not play a role in the initiation of plateau potentials, but is involved in sustaining them.
evidence: This is stated as an interpretation of the ncDHPR experiments.

claim: Ca2+ influx through Cav1.1 is involved in sustaining plateau potentials.
source: These data suggest that Ca2+ influx through Cav1.1 does not play a role in the initiation of plateau potentials, but is involved in sustaining them.
evidence: This is stated as an interpretation of the ncDHPR experiments.

claim: The duration of plateau potentials is shorter in ncDHPR muscle compared to wild-type muscle.
source: While there was no difference in the beginning or ending voltages of plateau potentials, the duration was shorter in ncDHPR muscle (Figure 6D and E, Table 2).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figures 6D and 6E and Table 2.

claim: The cause of the shorter plateau potential in ncDHPR muscle is an increase in the rate of repolarization.
source: The cause of the shorter plateau potential was an increase in the rate of repolarization (Table 2).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Table 2.

claim: When myotonia is triggered by treatment with 9-AC, 94% of fibers develop plateau potentials in response to a 200 ms injection of depolarizing current.
source: As shown in Figure 7A, when myotonia was triggered by the treatment of muscle with 9-AC, 94% of fibers (n = 53 fibers from eight mice) developed plateau potentials in response to a 200 ms injection of depolarizing current.
evidence: This is stated in the text with specific numbers and shown in Figure 7A.

claim: Following treatment with 40 µM ranolazine, 0/22 fibers from three mice developed plateau potentials after 200 ms current injection.
source: Following treatment with 40 µM ranolazine, 0/22 fibers from three mice developed plateau potentials after 200 ms current injection (Figure 7A, p<0.01 vs untreated).
evidence: This is stated in the text with specific numbers and statistical analysis, and shown in Figure 7A.

claim: 2 s of 20 Hz stimulation triggered plateau potentials in 46/55 fibers from 9-AC treated muscle.
source: 2 s of 20 Hz stimulation triggered plateau potentials in 46/55 fibers (n = 5 mice, Figure 7B).
evidence: This is stated in the text with specific numbers and shown in Figure 7B.

claim: Out of the 46 fibers with plateau potentials triggered by 20 Hz trains of stimuli, 11 fibers entered plateau potentials with limited (three or less myotonic APs) or no myotonia.
source: Out of the 46 fibers with plateau potentials triggered by 20 Hz trains of stimuli, 11 fibers entered plateau potentials with limited (three or less myotonic APs) or no myotonia.
evidence: This is stated in the text with specific numbers from the experiments.

claim: When 40 µM ranolazine was applied, plateau potentials developed in 0/68 fibers during 20 Hz stimulation.
source: When 40 µM ranolazine was applied, plateau potentials developed in 0/68 fibers (n = 5 mice, p<0.01 vs untreated, Figure 7B).
evidence: This is stated in the text with specific numbers and statistical analysis, and shown in Figure 7B.

claim: Ranolazine prevents plateau potentials by lessening depolarization of the mean membrane potential during 20 Hz stimulation.
source: These data suggest that ranolazine prevents plateau potentials by lessening depolarization of the mean membrane potential during the 20 Hz stimulation.
evidence: This is stated as an interpretation of the ranolazine experiments.

claim: In the absence of ranolazine, the mean membrane potential during the 500 ms prior to the plateau potential was −49.6 ± 2.5 mV.
source: In the absence of ranolazine, the mean membrane potential during the 500 ms prior to the plateau potential was −49.6 ± 2.5 mV (n = 5 muscles, 28 fibers).
evidence: This is stated in the text with specific values from the experiments.

claim: In the presence of 40 µM ranolazine, the mean membrane potential during 20 Hz stimulation was −56.2 ± 2.9 mV.
source: In the presence of 40 µM ranolazine, the mean membrane potential was less depolarized (−56.2 ± 2.9 mV, p<0.05 vs untreated, n = 5 muscles, Figure 7D).
evidence: This is stated in the text with specific values and statistical analysis, and shown in Figure 7D.

claim: The membrane potential for the 42 ms interspike interval before the 30th action potential was less depolarized following treatment with ranolazine.
source: The membrane potential for this 42 ms interspike interval before the 30th action potential was less depolarized following treatment with ranolazine (Figure 7C,F: −56.0 ± 2.3 vs −61.7 ± 3.0 mV, p<0.05).
evidence: This is stated in the text with specific values and statistical analysis, and shown in Figures 7C and 7F.

claim: Hyperpolarization of the interspike interval is largely responsible for hyperpolarization of the mean membrane potential during ranolazine treatment.
source: As the interspike interval accounts for 84% (42/50ms) of the time between spikes during 20 Hz stimulation, hyperpolarization of this interval is largely responsible for hyperpolarization of the mean membrane potential.
evidence: This is stated as an interpretation based on the timing calculations.

claim: Treatment with ranolazine decreased myotonia such that muscle was able to more rapidly relax following termination of stimulation.
source: As shown previously (Novak et al., 2015), treatment with ranolazine decreased myotonia such that muscle was able to more rapidly relax following termination of stimulation (Figure 8A).
evidence: This is stated in the text with a supporting citation and shown in Figure 8A.

claim: Treatment with ranolazine eliminated transient weakness in all five ClCadr mice tested.
source: In addition to lessening myotonia, treatment with ranolazine eliminated transient weakness in all five mice (Figure 8A and B, p<0.01 vs untreated at 16 s).
evidence: This is stated in the text with specific numbers and statistical analysis, and shown in Figures 8A and 8B.

claim: The elimination of both plateau potentials and transient weakness by ranolazine supports the hypothesis that plateau potentials are the mechanism underlying transient weakness in vivo.
source: The elimination of both plateau potentials and transient weakness by ranolazine supports the hypothesis that plateau potentials are the mechanism underlying transient weakness in vivo.
evidence: This is stated as an interpretation of the ranolazine experiments.

claim: Muscle from a mouse model of Becker disease undergoes a rapid transition between the states of hyperexcitability (myotonia) and inexcitability (due to plateau potentials).
source: Our data suggest that muscle from a mouse model of Becker disease undergoes a rapid transition between the states of hyperexcitability (myotonia) and inexcitability (due to plateau potentials), shown in Figure 9.
evidence: This is stated as an interpretation of the experimental findings and shown in Figure 9.

claim: During plateau potentials, fibers cannot generate action potentials in response to stimulation, providing an explanation for the drop in CMAP amplitude reported in patients.
source: During plateau potentials, fibers cannot generate action potentials in response to stimulation, providing an explanation for the drop in CMAP amplitude reported in patients (Ricker and Meinck, 1972; Brown, 1974; Aminoff et al., 1977; Deymeer et al., 1998; Drost et al., 2001; Modoni et al., 2011).
evidence: This is stated as an interpretation with supporting citations.

claim: Both myotonia (hyperexcitability) and plateau potentials (inexcitability) are caused by depolarization secondary to loss of muscle Cl- current.
source: The reason for the rapid transition between myotonia (hyperexcitability) and plateau potentials (inexcitability) is that both states are caused by depolarization secondary to loss of muscle Cl- current.
evidence: This is stated as an interpretation of the experimental findings.

claim: When depolarization is mild, Na+ channels are not inactivated, such that repetitive firing of action potentials is triggered.
source: The difference is one of degree: when depolarization is mild, Na+ channels are not inactivated, such that repetitive firing of action potentials is triggered.
evidence: This is stated as an interpretation of the experimental findings.

claim: When depolarization worsens, Na+ channels inactivate, such that inexcitability and paralysis ensue.
source: When depolarization worsens, Na+ channels inactivate, such that inexcitability and paralysis ensue.
evidence: This is stated as an interpretation of the experimental findings.

claim: A mean membrane potential of −44 mV appears to predict both entry into, as well as termination of, plateau potentials.
source: The midpoint of the difference between these values is close to −44 mV. In ClCadr muscle, the mean membrane potential prior to termination of plateau potentials was −46 mV, and in 9-AC treated muscle it was −45 mV. Thus, a mean membrane potential of −44 mV appears to predict both entry into, as well as termination of, plateau potentials.
evidence: This is stated as an interpretation based on the experimental measurements.

claim: In spinal motor neurons, CaV1.3 channels play a central role in the generation of plateau potentials that last many seconds.
source: In spinal motor neurons, CaV1.3 channels play a central role in the generation of plateau potentials that last many seconds (Alaburda et al., 2002; Heckman and Enoka, 2012; Hounsgaard, 2017).
evidence: This is stated with supporting citations to prior literature.

claim: NaPIC in muscle can activate and deactivate within 10 ms.
source: NaPIC in muscle can activate and deactivate within 10 ms (Gage et al., 1989).
evidence: This is stated with a supporting citation to prior literature.

claim: Kv channels begin to activate at voltages reached during plateau potentials.
source: Kv channels could participate in oscillations occurring during plateau potentials given that Kv conductance in muscle is large and the channels begin to activate at voltages reached during plateau potentials (Beam and Donaldson, 1983; DiFranco et al., 2012).
evidence: This is stated with supporting citations to prior literature.

claim: Plateau potentials in 9AC treated muscle were significantly shorter than in ClCadr muscle.
source: As an example of how such an approach might work, plateau potentials in 9AC treated muscle were significantly shorter than in ClCadr muscle.
evidence: This is stated as an observation from the experimental data.

claim: ClC-1 conductance is not completely blocked following application of 100 µM 9-AC.
source: The first is that ClC-1 conductance is not completely blocked following application of 100 µM 9-AC (Palade and Barchi, 1977).
evidence: This is stated with a supporting citation to prior literature.

claim: NaPIC current is larger in ClCadr muscle compared to wild-type muscle.
source: The second is that NaPIC current is larger in ClCadr muscle compared to wild-type muscle (used for the 9-AC model of myotonia) (Hawash et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated with a supporting citation to prior literature.

claim: In open label trials of ranolazine in both myotonia congenita and paramyotonia congenita, there were statistically significant reductions in the degree of self-reported weakness.
source: In open label trials of ranolazine in both myotonia congenita and paramyotonia congenita, there were statistically significant reductions in the degree of self-reported weakness (Arnold et al., 2017; Lorusso et al., 2019).
evidence: This is stated with supporting citations to prior literature.

claim: The clinical benefit of blocking Na+ channels in some diseases with myotonia may result, in part, from prevention of transient weakness secondary to development of plateau potentials.
source: Taken together, these data suggest that the clinical benefit of blocking Na+ channels in some diseases with myotonia may result, in part, from prevention of transient weakness secondary to development of plateau potentials.
evidence: This is stated as an interpretation of the combined experimental and clinical data.

claim: Blocking of Cav1.1 channels might reduce transient weakness by shortening the duration of plateau potentials.
source: Our data also raises the possibility that blocking of Cav1.1 channels might reduce transient weakness by shortening the duration of plateau potentials.
evidence: This is stated as a speculation based on the experimental findings.

claim: Mutations of NaV1.4 responsible for hyperkalemic periodic paralysis increase NaPIC.
source: Mutations of NaV1.4 responsible for hyperkalemic periodic paralysis increase NaPIC (Cannon et al., 1991; Cannon and Strittmatter, 1993a), which appears to play a central role in triggering the depolarization that underlies attacks of transient weakness (Lehmann-Horn et al., 1987; Jurkat-Rott et al., 2010; Cannon, 2015).
evidence: This is stated with supporting citations to prior literature.

claim: Increased NaPIC appears to play a central role in triggering the depolarization that underlies attacks of transient weakness in hyperkalemic periodic paralysis.
source: Mutations of NaV1.4 responsible for hyperkalemic periodic paralysis increase NaPIC (Cannon et al., 1991; Cannon and Strittmatter, 1993a), which appears to play a central role in triggering the depolarization that underlies attacks of transient weakness (Lehmann-Horn et al., 1987; Jurkat-Rott et al., 2010; Cannon, 2015).
evidence: This is stated with supporting citations to prior literature.

claim: Blocking NaPIC should be effective in treating hyperkalemic periodic paralysis.
source: This suggests that blocking NaPIC should be effective in treating hyperkalemic periodic paralysis.
evidence: This is stated as an inference from the role of NaPIC in hyperkalemic periodic paralysis.

claim: Treating patients with hyperkalemic periodic paralysis with Na+ channel blockers such as mexiletine was previously found to be ineffective.
source: However, treating patients with Na+ channel blockers that are effective in treating myotonia, such as mexiletine, was previously found to be ineffective (Ricker et al., 1983; Ricker et al., 1986).
evidence: This is stated with supporting citations to prior literature.

claim: Currents contributing to plateau potentials are present in wild-type muscle.
source: Currents contributing to plateau potentials are present in wild-type muscle; thus, they might contribute to depolarization in other muscle channelopathies with transient weakness, such as hyper- and hypokalemic periodic paralysis.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from the experimental findings.

claim: Currents contributing to plateau potentials might contribute to depolarization in other muscle channelopathies with transient weakness, such as hyper- and hypokalemic periodic paralysis.
source: Currents contributing to plateau potentials are present in wild-type muscle; thus, they might contribute to depolarization in other muscle channelopathies with transient weakness, such as hyper- and hypokalemic periodic paralysis.
evidence: This is stated as a speculation based on the experimental findings.

claim: 100 µM 9-AC blocks more than 95% of ClC-1 chloride channels in skeletal muscle.
source: This dose of 9-AC blocks more than 95% of ClC-1 chloride channels in skeletal muscle (Palade and Barchi, 1977) and has been used to model myotonia congenita both in vitro and in vivo (van Lunteren et al., 2011; Desaphy et al., 2013; Desaphy et al., 2014; Skov et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated with supporting citations to prior literature.

claim: 100 µM 9-AC has been used to model myotonia congenita both in vitro and in vivo.
source: This dose of 9-AC blocks more than 95% of ClC-1 chloride channels in skeletal muscle (Palade and Barchi, 1977) and has been used to model myotonia congenita both in vitro and in vivo (van Lunteren et al., 2011; Desaphy et al., 2013; Desaphy et al., 2014; Skov et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated with supporting citations to prior literature.

claim: Depolarizations lasting less than 1 s to a membrane potential close to −60 mV have been described in a toxin-induced model of hyperkalemic periodic paralysis and were termed plateau depolarizations.
source: Depolarizations lasting less than 1 s to a membrane potential close to −60 mV have been described in a toxin-induced model of hyperkalemic periodic paralysis and were termed plateau depolarizations (Cannon and Corey, 1993b).
evidence: This is stated with a supporting citation to prior literature.

claim: Prolonged depolarizations in spinal motor neurons can last many seconds and have been termed plateau potentials.
source: While the depolarizations we identified could be due to similar mechanisms as those described in hyperkalemic periodic paralysis, they seemed more similar to prolonged depolarizations in spinal motor neurons, which can last many seconds, and have been termed plateau potentials (Alaburda et al., 2002; Heckman and Enoka, 2012; Hounsgaard, 2017).
evidence: This is stated with supporting citations to prior literature.

claim: Ranolazine has been found to preferentially block NaPIC in brain, heart, peripheral nerve, and skeletal muscle.
source: Ranolazine has been found to preferentially block NaPIC in brain, heart, peripheral nerve, and skeletal muscle (El-Bizri et al., 2011; Kahlig et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated with supporting citations to prior literature.

claim: Ranolazine was effective in eliminating myotonia by blocking NaPIC while sparing enough fast-inactivating Na+ channels to allow for repetitive firing of action potentials triggered by current injection.
source: We previously found that ranolazine was effective in eliminating myotonia by blocking NaPIC while sparing enough fast-inactivating Na+ channels to allow for repetitive firing of action potentials triggered by current injection (Novak et al., 2015; Hawash et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated with supporting citations to prior literature.

claim: NaPIC contributes to repetitive firing occurring during myotonia.
source: We recently determined that NaPIC contributes to repetitive firing occurring during myotonia (Hawash et al., 2017; Metzger et al., 2020).
evidence: This is stated with supporting citations to prior literature.

claim: NaPIC is present in normal skeletal muscle and likely derives from modal gating in which a small subset of Nav1.4 channels reversibly enter a mode lacking fast-inactivation.
source: NaPIC is present in normal skeletal muscle and likely derives from modal gating in which a small subset of Nav1.4 channels reversibly enter a mode lacking fast-inactivation (Patlak and Ortiz, 1986; Gage et al., 1989).
evidence: This is stated with supporting citations to prior literature.

claim: K+ build-up in the transverse (t)-tubules depolarizes the K+ equilibrium potential.
source: Previously, the only identified contributor to depolarization of the interspike membrane potential was K+ build-up in the transverse (t)-tubules (invaginations of the sarcolemma), which depolarizes the K+ equilibrium potential (Adrian and Bryant, 1974; Adrian and Marshall, 1976; Wallinga et al., 1999; Fraser et al., 2011).
evidence: This is stated with supporting citations to prior literature.

claim: Block of NaPIC lessens depolarization of the interspike membrane potential, suggesting that NaPIC is activated during this interval.
source: The finding that block of NaPIC lessens depolarization of the interspike membrane potential suggests that NaPIC is activated during this interval.
evidence: This is stated as an interpretation of the ranolazine experiments.

claim: Activation of NaPIC combines with K+ build-up in t-tubules to depolarize muscle to a mean membrane potential of −44 mV during myotonia, such that a plateau potential is triggered.
source: We hypothesize that activation of NaPIC combines with K+ build-up in t-tubules to depolarize muscle to a mean membrane potential of −44 mV during myotonia, such that a plateau potential is triggered.
evidence: This is stated as a hypothesis based on the experimental findings.

claim: Members of the TRP ion channel family are expressed in skeletal muscle.
source: Members of the TRP ion channel family are expressed in skeletal muscle (Brinkmeier, 2011; Gailly, 2012), and we recently found that activation of TRPV4 plays a role in triggering percussion myotonia (Dupont et al., 2020).
evidence: This is stated with supporting citations to prior literature.

claim: Activation of TRPV4 plays a role in triggering percussion myotonia.

claim: Depolarization has previously been found to cause widening of action potentials.
source: This widening of the spike-form was likely due to failure of the membrane potential to fully repolarize between action potentials, given that depolarization has previously been found to cause widening of action potentials (Renaud and Light, 1992; Yensen et al., 2002; Miranda et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated with supporting citations to prior literature.

claim: In wild-type littermate controls, ramp depolarization following block of Na+, K+, and Cl− channels triggered a large, inward Ca2+ current, which began to activate at −15.1 ± 6.9 mV with a mean amplitude of 165 ± 46 nA.

claim: In oscillations in membrane potential in motor neurons, the oscillations are caused by a balance between two voltage-gated ion channels: one promoting depolarization and one promoting hyperpolarization.
source: In motor neurons, oscillations in membrane potential are caused by a balance between two voltage-gated ion channels: one promoting depolarization and one promoting hyperpolarization (Iglesias et al., 2011; Sciamanna and Wilson, 2011; Nardelli et al., 2017).
